LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_None.label: no type
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_AND.label: Logic AND
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_AND.description:
Outputs a signal only while every connected input has one. Let a single input go quiet and the output goes dark with it. Power behaves the same way: current passes only when all inputs are live.
Use it when something should happen only if several conditions line up at once. Turn on a turret, say, but only if the motion sensor fired AND night has fallen.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_OR.label: Logic OR
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_OR.description:
Outputs a signal if at least ONE connected input has one. Power behaves the same way: current flows as long as any input is live.
Use it when any of several reasons should be enough. Sound the alert if the fire sensor trips OR the motion sensor does — whichever gets there first.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_XOR.label: Logic XOR
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_XOR.description:
Outputs a signal when the inputs DISAGREE: one has a signal, the other does not. If both are on, or both are off, the output stays dark. Power behaves the same way.
Handy when the disagreement itself is what matters: catch the moment two sensors stop telling the same story and raise an alert.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_NAND.label: Logic NAND
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_NAND.description:
The opposite of AND: the output is on ALL the time, except when every input has a signal at once. Signals only — no power passes through.
Good for things that should run by default and stop when conditions meet. Ventilation keeps the air moving, then rests once every door is shut.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_NOR.label: Logic NOR
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_NOR.description:
The opposite of OR: there is a signal only while NO input has one. The moment anything speaks up, the output goes dark. Signals only.
This is your "all quiet" condition. Light the workshop only while both the fire sensor and the motion sensor have nothing to report.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_XNOR.label: Logic XNOR
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_XNOR.description:
The opposite of XOR: there is a signal while the inputs AGREE — both on, or both off. The moment they differ, the output goes dark. Signals only.
Useful for watching that things stay consistent: as long as two sensors say the same thing, the circuit treats the situation as normal.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Register.label: Register
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Register.description:
Behaves like a latching button. Each new signal flips the output to the other state: on becomes off, off becomes on. Between signals it holds that state on its own.
Use it to switch something on and off with the same signal. One pressure plate lights the room; press it again and the light goes out. Needs power.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Splitter.label: Splitter
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Splitter.description:
Copies one signal into several. Feed a signal (or power) into the input and it goes out through every output at once, identical and simultaneous.
Use it when one sensor should drive several blocks: a single motion sensor turning on the lights, the turret and the speaker together.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_SensorLight.label: Light sensor
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_SensorLight.description:
Watches the light level on its own tile. When the light matches what you set, it gives a signal and passes power from input to output, acting as a switch of its own.
The classic use is street lighting: lamps come on as dusk falls and go out in the morning, without a single order from you.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_SensorMotion.label: Motion sensor
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_SensorMotion.description:
Reacts to movement in the area around it. In the settings you choose who to notice (colonists, animals, enemies, prisoners and others) and how wide the area reaches.
While a matching target is inside, it gives a signal and passes power from input to output. Good for lights that follow people, doors that open themselves, or an alarm when strangers turn up.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_SensorTemperature.label: Temperature sensor
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_SensorTemperature.descript:
Watches the temperature on its own tile. When it matches the condition you set, the sensor gives a signal and passes power from input to output.
Use it to let the climate look after itself: the heater comes on when a room gets cold, the cooler when it gets hot. The condition is set in the settings.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_SensorCurrent.label: Power sensor
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_SensorCurrent.description:
Wire the input into your grid and the sensor watches how much spare power it has, or how much charge is left in the batteries. When the figure matches your condition, it gives a signal.
It only watches — no power passes through it. Use it to let a circuit answer a shortage on its own: shed the non-essentials when the batteries run low, or have the speaker warn you.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_SensorPressure.label: Pressure sensor
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_SensorPollution.label: Pollution sensor
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_SensorPollution.descriptio:
Checks whether there is pollution in the chosen area. If there is, it gives a signal and passes power from input to output.
Handy for catching a problem before it spreads — raise an alert once the filth creeps up on your crops. The area is set in the settings.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_SensorFire.label: Fire sensor
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_SensorFire.description:
Reacts when a fire starts in the chosen area. While anything is burning it gives a signal and passes power from input to output.
The foundation of a fire-response circuit: that signal can sound the speaker, cut power to a section, or open doors so people can get out. The area is set in the settings.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Switch.label: Switch
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Switch.description:
A switch driven by a signal. While the control input has a signal, power passes from the electrical input to the electrical output; when the signal stops, the circuit opens.
This is how you hand power over to logic: any sensor or circuit gains the ability to switch a whole section of the grid on and off.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Selector.label: Selector
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Selector.description:
Sends the incoming power to ONE of two outputs — left or right. Each new signal on the control input flips it to the other side.
Power always goes to one place, never both at once, which makes it easy to share a supply between two consumers in turn. Every switch-over also sends a short pulse to the output.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Analyzer.label: Analyzer
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Timer.label: Timer
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Timer.description:
Holds a signal back for a set time. When a signal arrives it waits out the delay you configured, and only then passes it on.
If the signal is still there by then, the output holds too; if it has already stopped, the output gives a short pulse instead. Use it so lights do not snap off instantly, doors close a moment later, and events run in sequence with pauses between them. Needs power.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Memory.label: Memory
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Memory.description:
Stores a number. From a plain signal it remembers 1 or 0; from blocks that carry a number (the selector, the math block, another memory) it remembers that number, and holds it until the next change.
The current value is set in the settings. Every time the value changes it sends a short pulse to the output, so the rest of the circuit knows the data has been updated. Needs power.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Math.label: Math block
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Math.description:
Works with numbers. It takes the number from the left input (the first) and the right one (the second) and performs the operation you chose: add, subtract, multiply, divide, compare and more. The result goes to the output.
Comparisons turn a number back into a plain signal — "steel below 200", and the circuit raises the alert by itself. The operation is chosen in the settings.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Multitool.label: Multitool
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Multitool.description:
A jack of all trades: one building, several modes to pick from in its settings.
It can count items in an area, switch a neighbouring device on and off by signal, open and close doors, count crops ready for harvest, count pawns by filter, and measure how full your storage is. Reach for it whenever a circuit needs to touch ordinary buildings and colony stockpiles.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Screen.label: Screen
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Screen.description:
Shows a single digit of the number arriving at its input.
Several screens fed from one source form a display: the first one connected shows the units, the second the tens, and so on. Negative numbers get a minus sign. That is how you put your steel reserve, the temperature, or the reading of any number-carrying block up on a wall. Needs power.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Clock.label: Clock
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Clock.description:
Gives a signal at a chosen time of day. In the settings you pick an hour or a span of hours and a condition (before, after, within a range and so on) — while local time matches it, the output carries a signal.
Use it for schedules: lights in the evening, machines running only by day, non-essentials shut down overnight. Needs power.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Loudspeaker.label: Loudspeaker
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Loudspeaker.description:
On a signal it puts an in-game notification on screen — blue or red, with your own heading and text.
This is the voice of the whole circuit: a sensor or a calculation can tell you about a fire, a power shortage or an empty store, so you do not have to watch the readings yourself. The signal also carries on to the output. Needs power.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Diode.label: Diode
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Diode.description:
Lets power through in one direction only: from input to output while the input side has power to spare, and it opens the circuit when there is none.
Use it to split a grid into sections — hand your surplus to a backup branch without letting that branch pull power back. The control signal switches the diode on and off, and its output carries a signal whenever current is actually passing.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_SignalGen.label: Signal generator
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_SignalGen.description:
Holds a signal on its output the whole time it is running. This is your basic source of a constant "on" for circuits.
Use it when something needs a signal that never stops: holding a door open, keeping a block from switching itself off, or feeding a condition that is always true. A logic input can interrupt it. Needs power.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_TickGen.label: Tick generator
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_TickGen.description:
Sends out signals in an even rhythm, again and again, with the same gap between them.
This is the heartbeat of a circuit: counters count by its pulses, sequences step through by them, and repeating actions fire on them. A logic input can interrupt the beat. Needs power.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Crafter.label: Crafter
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Crafter.description:
Takes a colonist's place at a bench and works through that bench's queue. What to make is set in the bench itself — there is nothing to configure on the block.
While it stands there, colonists will not use that bench. Its settings choose which storage to draw materials from and where finished goods go. The block's level is raised with materials: the higher it goes, the faster it works and the better it builds.
It works as a real worker at the bench: every recipe is available, butchering and smelting included, and so are benches from other mods. Speed, quality and fuel use are worked out by the same rules that apply to a colonist.
Materials are only taken from the chosen storage — the block does not go fetching them from across the base. Finished goods go straight into the destination storage.
The block reports its own state on the output as a number: 0 — no power 1 — on, nothing to do 2 — switched off by signal 3 — working 4 — started an item (brief pulse) 5 — finished an item (brief pulse) 6 — the bench queue is empty 7 — not enough materials 8 — nowhere to put finished goods
The logic converter is what catches a particular number and turns it into a plain signal.
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Converter.label: Logic converter
LanguageData.RimLogic_Type_Converter.description:
Translates one kind of signal into the other. It can wait for a plain signal or for one specific number, and send back either a plain signal or a number you choose.
Its main use is catching a particular block state and turning it into a plain signal — "the crafter says it is out of materials" becomes a signal for the speaker. It works the other way round too: tag an ordinary event with a number.
